findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal axis and intervals. No acute ST-T changes.
Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging gait and distractibility; witnessed event with eyes closed and retained responsiveness
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs and observe an event
action_criteria.rationale: Three weeks of right leg weakness and shaking episodes: the diagnosis rests on positive signs such as the Hoover sign and collapsing weakness and on the semiology of an observed event, not on the exclusion of other disease (DSM-5 criterion B).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual events recorded on video with no EEG change and a normal interictal record
action_criteria.label: Record the habitual events on video-EEG
action_criteria.rationale: She has shaking episodes every two to three days, and a maternal aunt has generalized epilepsy. Recording a habitual event without ictal change reaches the ILAE documented level of certainty and assesses co-occurring epilepsy, as the AAN guideline advises. Without the recording, the positive signs and the semiology of witnessed events support the diagnosis at a lower ILAE level of certainty (LaFrance 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No lesion explaining the right leg weakness
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI without contrast, once, if a structural question remains
action_criteria.rationale: The leg weakness began on waking three weeks ago and the ED CT was normal; preserved reflexes, flexor plantars and the positive signs already answer the structural question, so a single non-contrast scan is defensible but does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bleeding risk with ibuprofen and QT and sedation risk with hydroxyzine alongside sertraline; nothing was started for the events
action_criteria.label: Review the current medicines for interactions
action_criteria.rationale: No antiseizure drug or benzodiazepine has been started for her events, so the review does not change the plan; sertraline with ibuprofen and with hydroxyzine are worth noting.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Quantifies mood, anxiety and symptom burden to guide therapy; does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment, if it will guide therapy
action_criteria.rationale: It can quantify her anxiety, dissociative and trauma-related symptoms to target psychological treatment, but it does not make the diagnosis and is the most expensive item on this pathway, so it is justified only when the result will shape therapy.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background evidence only, with no bearing on this patient's work-up
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on FND diagnosis and treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Reading on positive signs and treatment trials is background knowledge, not a clinical step; nothing in this patient's diagnosis or plan depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat CT after the normal emergency department scan, repeat MRI, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Start or escalate antiseizure medication for the functional seizures.
Give benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (mixed: functional right leg weakness and functional seizures) based on the right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging monoplegic gait and distractibility, and on the semiology of the habitual events, confirmed on video-EEG where recorded, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).

Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid generalized anxiety disorder. Re-establish the psychiatric follow-up that has lapsed for a year, with trauma-informed care given the childhood sexual abuse.

Give the patient, family and ward a written plan for typical events: keep safe, do not restrain, wait for the event to end, and do not give emergency benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.

avoided_actions.rationale: She has no syncope, palpitations or chest pain, and the events are shaking with retained responsiveness; an ECG adds nothing.
No murmur, syncope or embolic question is raised; an echocardiogram answers nothing in this patient.
She stays responsive during the shaking and has no syncope or palpitations; nothing suggests an arrhythmia.
A head CT in the emergency department during this illness was normal; repeating it answers no new question and adds radiation.
She is afebrile with no inflammatory or encephalopathic feature; a lumbar puncture would add iatrogenic risk and answer no question.
FDG-PET has no diagnostic role in functional seizures or functional weakness and answers no question in this patient.

The right leg weakness has normal reflexes, tone and bulk with a positive Hoover sign and collapsing weakness; it is not neuromuscular, and a normal EMG would only feed the search for an organic cause.
Sensory loss of the whole right leg ending at the inguinal crease, with proprioception intact on distraction, is not a question about the somatosensory pathway.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder) with motor symptoms (right leg weakness) and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures

differential.key_features: Recurrent shaking episodes with falls and a maternal aunt with generalized epilepsy. Habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; co-occurring epilepsy remains possible in about one in five patients with functional seizures.

Right leg weakness noticed on waking raises an anterior cerebral artery territory stroke; preserved and symmetric reflexes, flexor plantars, a positive Hoover sign with collapsing weakness and a dragging gait without circumduction argue against it.

differential.diagnosis: Multiple sclerosis or another structural lesion of the brain or spinal cord
differential.key_features: Leg weakness with sensory loss in a young adult raises demyelination or a cord lesion; normal reflexes and tone, flexor plantars, normal bladder function, proprioception intact on distraction and the positive functional signs are incompatible with a corticospinal or dorsal column lesion.

key_clinical_evidence: The right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging monoplegic gait and distractibility are validated rule-in signs; the sensory loss ending at the inguinal crease and the Romberg sway are supportive only.

The witnessed event (eyes tightly closed and resisting opening, irregular waxing and waning shaking, responsive to commands, immediately alert) has functional semiology, and a habitual event was recorded on video-EEG without ictal change: the ILAE documented level of certainty.
A maternal aunt with generalized epilepsy modestly raises the prior probability of epilepsy but does not decide the nature of her recorded events.

Work stress, relationship conflict, a friend's cancer diagnosis and a history of childhood abuse are supportive context and treatment targets; a stressor is neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A second-degree family history of epilepsy does not make her events epileptic; the habitual event recorded on video-EEG without ictal change answers the question.
red_herrings.data_point: Maternal aunt with generalized tonic-clonic epilepsy on levetiracetam
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on an epileptic cause and start antiseizure drugs before the events are recorded

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. Diagnosis requires positive rule-in signs on examination; psychiatric history is relevant for treatment planning, not for diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Generalized anxiety disorder, past major depression and childhood sexual abuse
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions (MS, migraine, epilepsy) also flare with stress. Stress at onset is supportive context, not a diagnostic substitute for the positive rule-in signs.
red_herrings.data_point: Work stress, relationship conflict and a close friend's cancer diagnosis before onset
red_herrings.intended_effect: Make the diagnosis from the stressors alone, without positive signs or typical event semiology

findings.result: Right hip extension weak on direct testing, full strength during left hip flexion against resistance.
Right hip flexion, knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion start with full resistance and then collapse, graded 2-3/5 and inconsistent on repeat testing.
Right leg dragged behind with the hip externally rotated, without circumduction or knee buckling.
Right heel-to-shin moves smoothly when she is distracted, and leg function improves while she walks and talks.

Bilateral arm shaking for about 90 seconds, irregular and waxing and waning, with the eyes tightly closed and resisting opening; she followed verbal commands during the event and was immediately alert afterwards.

Light-touch and pinprick loss over the whole right leg with a sharp boundary at the inguinal crease, toe proprioception reported as reduced but intact when tested with distraction, and exaggerated Romberg sway without falling; not counted as rule-in signs.
Reflexes 2+ and symmetric including the right patellar reflex, flexor plantars, no clonus; normal tone, no pronator drift.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness: right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging monoplegic gait and distractibility of the right leg deficit. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion. The event semiology (eyes closed and resisting opening, irregular waxing and waning shaking, retained responsiveness, immediate recovery) is typical of functional seizures; the examination does not by itself exclude epileptic seizures.

interactions: Sertraline with ibuprofen: SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin and NSAIDs injure the gastric mucosa; increased risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding with regular combined use. Consider gastroprotection or a non-NSAID analgesic.

Sertraline with hydroxyzine: additive QT prolongation is possible; hydroxyzine also adds sedation. Keep hydroxyzine at the lowest effective dose (adult maximum 100 mg daily) and avoid other QT-prolonging drugs.
current_medications.proposed: Sertraline 100 mg once daily; hydroxyzine 25 mg as needed up to three times daily; ibuprofen 400 mg as needed
current_medications.summary: Two moderate interactions: sertraline with ibuprofen (gastrointestinal bleeding risk) and sertraline with hydroxyzine (QT prolongation, sedation).
warnings: Hydroxyzine: sedation and anticholinergic effects; avoid in patients with known QT prolongation or uncorrected hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia.

activating_procedures.hyperventilation: Performed for 3 minutes. Normal buildup of diffuse slowing with prompt recovery. No epileptiform discharges provoked. Patient reported feeling lightheaded but no clinical event occurred.
activating_procedures.photic_stimulation: Performed at standard flash frequencies 1-30 Hz. Normal photic driving response. No photoparoxysmal response.

artifacts.description: During clinical event, obscures some channels but underlying rhythms discernible on referential montage
Intermittent, correlates with patient anxiety, does not obscure posterior dominant rhythm

background.overall: Continuous inpatient video-EEG for 24 hours, international 10-20 system. Normal, symmetric background in wakefulness and sleep.
background.posterior_dominant_rhythm: 10 Hz alpha rhythm, symmetric, well-organized, reactive to eye opening
background.sleep_features: Stage N2 sleep with vertex waves and sleep spindles; normal architecture

findings.morphology: Generalized shaking of the arms and legs with the eyes closed, irregular in amplitude, lasting 1 min 15 s; she answered questions during the event. Movement artifact over most channels; the posterior alpha rhythm remained discernible on the referential montage. No evolving rhythmic activity and no postictal slowing.

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL video-EEG. One habitual event was recorded (generalized shaking with the eyes closed, 1 min 15 s) without ictal EEG change before, during or after the event; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted during the event. No interictal epileptiform discharges. No electrographic seizures.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Defines levels of certainty for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; the documented level requires a typical event recorded on video-EEG without ictal EEG change.
results.source: LaFrance WC Jr et al. Epilepsia 2013;54:2005-2018

results.finding: For functional seizures: assess for co-occurring epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, taper antiseizure medication without another indication, avoid benzodiazepines, and offer psychological therapy, which is possibly effective.
CBT added to standardised medical care did not reduce dissociative seizure frequency at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured CBT.
results.source: Goldstein LH et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:491-505

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

additional_observations: Technique: sagittal T1, axial T2, axial and sagittal FLAIR, DWI with ADC, SWI; no contrast administered
Normal ventricular system size and configuration
No mass lesion or space-occupying process
Normal brain parenchymal volume for age
Normal flow voids in major intracranial vessels
mri.impression: Normal non-contrast MRI of the brain. No restricted diffusion, no T2/FLAIR signal abnormality, no mass effect.

clinical_pearls: Hoover sign is the most validated positive clinical sign for functional leg weakness and can be demonstrated at bedside
Ictal eye closure that resists opening favors a functional seizure over an epileptic seizure, but no single feature is diagnostic
FND is one of the most common reasons for neurological outpatient referrals, affecting up to 16% of neurology clinic patients
A family history of epilepsy modestly raises the prior probability of epilepsy but does not decide the nature of the events; a recorded habitual event does
metadata.difficulty_rationale: The required work-up is the examination; a video-EEG can confirm the events. A normal ED CT, a wake-up onset of leg weakness and an aunt with epilepsy invite repeat imaging and an epilepsy work-up; the main task is explaining the diagnosis and re-engaging psychiatric care.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Crystal Morris is a 34-year-old right-handed woman and elementary school teacher who presents as an inpatient transfer from the emergency department after three weeks of progressive right leg weakness and recurrent episodes of uncontrollable shaking. The symptoms began abruptly three weeks ago when she awoke one morning and found that her right leg felt heavy and difficult to move. She reports that she was unable to bear weight on the right leg and fell twice that first day. Over the following days, the weakness persisted and she began using a cane provided by a friend. Approximately one week after the onset of weakness, she experienced her first shaking episode while at home: her arms and legs began trembling, she fell to the floor, and the episode lasted roughly two minutes. Her boyfriend witnessed the event and reports that she appeared awake during the episode and could respond to her name, though she later described feeling detached from her body. She has since had five additional similar episodes, occurring roughly every two to three days, sometimes triggered by emotional stress or arguments. Emergency medical services were called during the third episode and she was brought to the emergency department, where a CT head was normal and she was discharged with neurology follow-up. She returned to the ED two days ago after two episodes occurred in the same day, one at home and one in the waiting room of her primary care physician's office. The waiting room episode was witnessed by nursing staff, who noted bilateral arm shaking with eyes closed and no loss of continence. She was admitted for further workup. She denies headache, visual changes, numbness or tingling in the upper extremities, bowel or bladder incontinence, fever, weight loss, or recent illness. She reports significant emotional distress related to work stress, relationship difficulties, and learning of a close friend's cancer diagnosis shortly before symptom onset. She was previously seen by a psychiatrist for anxiety and depression but has not had regular follow-up in the past year.

neurological_exam.additional: During the examination, the patient had a paroxysmal episode of bilateral upper extremity shaking lasting approximately 90 seconds. Eyes were tightly closed with resistance to opening, and she appeared to retain awareness (responded to verbal commands during the event). The shaking was irregular, variable in amplitude, and waxed and waned. No tonic phase, no cyanosis, no tongue biting, no urinary incontinence. She was immediately alert and conversant after the episode with no post-ictal confusion.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing normal bilaterally. Heel-to-shin testing normal on the left; patient reports inability to perform on the right due to weakness, but when distracted the right leg moves smoothly to the shin. No intention tremor. Rapid alternating movements intact in upper extremities.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Pupils equal, round, reactive to light 3mm to 2mm bilaterally. Fundoscopic exam normal, no papilledema. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus or diplopia. CN V: Sensation intact to light touch in all three divisions bilaterally. Masseter strength symmetric. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with activation, no facial droop. CN VIII: Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically. CN XI: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue midline, no fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.gait: Patient walks with a dragging right leg pattern. The gait is effortful-appearing but non-physiological — the leg drags behind with the hip externally rotated but knee does not buckle. When distracted during conversation while ambulating, leg function intermittently improves. No circumduction. Romberg testing: marked swaying with eyes closed but catches herself repeatedly without falling (positive for functional sway). Tandem gait not attempted by patient due to reported weakness.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Affect is anxious but cooperative. Speech is fluent with normal rate, rhythm, and prosody. No dysarthria. Attention intact, able to recite months of the year backward. Memory 3/3 immediate and delayed recall. No aphasia. Fund of knowledge intact.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal in all extremities, no spasticity or rigidity. Right lower extremity: give-way weakness pattern noted in hip flexion, knee extension, and ankle dorsiflexion, with initial resistance to full strength followed by sudden collapse of effort. Formal testing yields 2-3/5 in these muscle groups with inconsistency on repeat testing. Left lower extremity: 5/5 throughout. Upper extremities: 5/5 bilaterally. Hoover sign positive on the right: voluntary right hip extension is weak on direct testing, but involuntary right hip extension is strong when she flexes the left hip against resistance. No pronator drift in upper extremities.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally (including right side despite reported weakness), Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses are flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Patient reports decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in the entire right leg up to the inguinal crease, with a sharp non-dermatomal boundary at the crease. Vibration and proprioception are reported as diminished in the right toes, but testing with distraction shows intact proprioception. Left leg sensation intact throughout. Upper extremity sensation intact bilaterally.
